7 Lessons From Riot CFO Mark Sottosanti
0
7 Lessons From Riot CFO Mark Sottosanti, Including How Arcane Season 2 Effectively Broke Even
Business
Oct 19
Written By
Michail Katkoff
Jen Donahoe
and
Eric Kress
had a conversation with
Mark Sottosanti
, CFO at
Riot Games
, on Arcane’s economics, Riot’s mobile wins in China, their 5-for-7 launch record, and why Riot keeps its next games secret.
In 2012, Mark Sottosanti was running a small hedge fund and had no plans to change jobs. He had spent two years playing League of Legends with his son, and a visit to Riot’s offices turned into meetings with Riot’s leaders. They had been searching for a head of monetization for a long time, and every candidate with free-to-play experience came from Korean MMOs, Facebook or mobile games, where monetization ran too aggressively for Riot’s culture. Mark offered to help part-time, fell for the people, and wound down his fund to take the job.
I (this is me,
Jen
writing) worked at Riot from 2018 to 2021, where I helped set up the mobile publishing team and launch Teamfight Tactics (TFT) as Riot’s first mobile game, and I got to know Mark during those years. When Mark reached out to my co-host Eric Kress, Kress put him at the top of his list and brought me in to run the conversation with him.
Mark has now spent 14 years at Riot and has been CFO since 2021. In that time, Riot went from one game to seven launches, five live games with full dev teams, and about 20 offices worldwide. He has also logged thousands of hours in TFT and finished a few sets at Grandmaster. Here are the seven lessons from our conversation that I believe matter most.

I seriously recommend listening to the full conversation; if not for the insights, then at least to hear Kress taking on Mark in some break-even jousting...
1. Arcane Season 2, effectively, broke even
Kress opened by pointing to reports that Arcane was not profitable. Mark confirmed that Season 1 “cost Riot a lot of money.” Netflix and other streamers would not cover Riot’s costs at the time because Riot had no reputation in animation. Season 2 changed the math, helped by Riot getting much better at letting players buy their favorite Arcane characters as skins.
“Season two was effectively break even when you include the incremental impact on skin sales.” Mark Sottosanti
I asked what counts toward break-even: skins alone or new players too. Mark said Riot counts all of it. Riot books the payments from Netflix and any other streamer. It measures how an Arcane skin sells against a regular skin and credits the difference to the show. It also compares new player growth during the show’s run against what its models predicted without Arcane.
Mark’s rule for every entertainment project is to strive for break-even, “because if we can achieve break-even, then all the ecosystem benefit is pure upside.” When a project misses, Riot tracks cost per viewer hour to guide the next investment.
Mark said that for future projects, “all the production costs would potentially be covered by the distribution partner” if Riot goes with Netflix or another streaming service, because Riot now has the reputation.
My read: Riot’s attribution math is the part every studio can copy.
Skin uplift against a regular skin and player growth against forecast work for any live game with a cosmetic store. Riot also shows how a first show buys the reputation that gets partners to fund the second.
Arcane Jinx in League of Legends. Image: Riot Games

2. Riot’s mobile wins run through China, and Valorant Mobile succeeds there with zero loot boxes
“Riot has three of the top 15 mobile games in China”
Fight for the Golden Spatula (TFTish), Wild Rift, and Valorant Mobile are all top 15 mobile games in China. Technically, all three are publishing arrangements with Tencent. Wild Rift is developed and published jointly with a Tencent division. Tencent built and publishes Valorant Mobile and Golden Spatula on Riot’s IP. These arrangements sit apart from licensing, which Riot avoids because “we are the only stewards of our IP that will ever be really happy with how it gets used.”
Mark gave two reasons it works. Tencent has deep mobile publishing capabilities, and “they earn their share of revenue.” Players in China also play hardcore games on mobile, often because they grew up without a PC or console. The gameplay stays “100% the same,” and Valorant Mobile runs with no loot boxes and no pay-to-win. Tencent had questions about that model at first.
“Tencent has realized that our games thrive with the monetization systems that they were built for.” Mark Sottosanti
When I was at Riot, the hard part was getting a company of PC players to see that players around the world love high-quality mobile games. Mark called traditional mobile “the antithesis” of what Riot does well, and credited me and others with helping Riot see that mobile needs its own publishing expertise.
My read: Riot proved two China models work.
Joint development works, as Wild Rift shows. So does handing a strong Western game and IP to Tencent to make it specific for China, which is how Golden Spatula and Valorant Mobile found their success. If you hold a strong IP, a publishing partner who adapts your game for China is a real path, as long as you hold the line on gameplay and monetization the way Riot did.
VALORANT Mobile key art (China). Image: Tencent Games / Riot Games

3. Riot has hit on 5 of its 7 launches without shrinking the League's team
Riot ran on one game for 10 years. Every time people started work on a new game, a League crisis or opportunity pulled them back within a few months. Then Riot shipped four games in two years: Valorant, TFT, Wild Rift and Legends of Runeterra. By Mark’s count, five of Riot’s seven launches are hits: League, Valorant
